title: AI in Microscopy: A BioImaging Guide
text:
Welcome
AI in Microscopy is an interactive online textbook intended to introduce biologists and microscopists to the fundamentals of artificial intelligence and machine learning.
The table of contents on the left can be used to navigate the book. Subsections of each chapter appear as a clickable menu on the right side of each chapter page. Key terms in each chapter are highlighted as links to the Glossary page. The upper left menu contains a toggle for using the website in dark mode.
A free PDF of the textbook can be downloaded from the upper left menu. Note that this PDF lacks some of the functionality of the online interactive book.
The source code for this textbook is available on GitHub. All content is licensed under BSD 3-Clause, except where noted otherwise.

title: 1  Preface
text:
The rapid advancement of microscopy, further fueled by parallel developments in related technologies such as probe chemistry, molecular biology, and image analysis methods, has propelled bioimaging to the forefront of life science studies1. In fact, many life scientists now fully expect to visualize intricate biological processes in the context of a whole, living organism—a prospect deemed impossible a mere decade ago.
This seemingly limitless possibility has greatly amplified the complexity of the questions that can be probed. Likewise, it demands a significant degree of forethought in the design of biological experiments2,3 to ensure that the maximal amount of biological information can be extracted from the acquired data. At the same time, the wealth of information contained in modern bioimage data can now often exceed the grasp of a human observer. This thus requires computational means to aid in data interpretation. In other words, the ever-expanding and multifaceted field of artificial intelligence (AI) can no longer be separated from bioimaging. Yet the absence of a comprehensive resource to systematically explore how AI can enhance bioimaging prevents many in the community from taking advantage of this indispensable technology. This textbook therefore aims to demystify AI in its many forms and outline proper use cases thereof to facilitate biological discovery. We have specifically contextualized the textbook for our two target audiences: microscopists and biologists. New AI and machine learning (ML) tools often fail to tailor explanations and tutorials for the very users that will ultimately effectuate scientific discovery. We hope this textbook will bridge that gap.
As the chapters of this book will collectively demonstrate, AI now plays an indispensable role in the four main stages of the microscopy experimental workflow (Figure 1.1): project design, tool-building, execution of experiments, and data modeling. The microscopist must optimize each of these stages in concert to maximize the usefulness of their data2,3. That optimization can be enhanced by AI tools, which are capable of everything from generating new ideas for experiments to maxizing the information in noisy images.






Figure 1.1: AI impacts every aspect of the microscopy workflow. The experimental process represents a cycle through four distinct phases: experimental design, constructing systems and workflows, testing hypotheses using these workflows, and analyzing their outputs to develop new models that inform new experiments. AI holds the capacity to impact each phase of this cycle. See also AI@HHMI.



To guide researchers just getting started with AI, the first section of this book focuses on introducing the core concepts of AI, large language models (LLMs), and the computational architectures that underpin these technologies. Chapter 2 will introduce the basic principles behind AI and ML as a gateway for those less familiar with this topic. In the experimental workflow, modern hypotheses can now drive a project design so complex that AI may be required to design the tools needed to tackle the experimental challenge. As will be discussed in Chapter 3, this can be accomplished by using LLMs as assistants. Chapter 4 will further explain the construction of AI models.
The next section focuses on extending microscopy hardware with AI. To render a microscope “smart”, i.e., for it to perform an experiment with minimal or no human intervention, ML software first needs to be trained on extensive and high-quality training data. The collection and design of training data will be covered in Chapter 5. Chapter 6 will discuss the implementation of AI and ML to enhance the capabilities of existing microscopes denoising and other image restoration techniques. Likewise, AI and ML models can be designed to control event-driven image acquisition to visualize biological events that are rare and/or photosensitive (Chapter 7).
The final section will address processing and analyzing microscopy data in order to extract biological information beyond what is achievable through human observation alone. Chapter 8 will focus on helping readers find and use available open-source tools. When those existing tools are insufficient, Chapter 9 seeks to further widen the horizon by discussing the process of training new models for specific image processing and analysis tasks. Finally, Chapter 10 will address the question of when a model is performing well enough. This important step pinpoints potential weaknesses of the analysis approach, thereby placing results in meaningful context.
We conclude with Chapter 11, which summarizes the core concepts and aims to inspire readers to begin taking full advantage of the promise of the new era of AI and ML. To close the loop, we also hope that by equipping readers with the proper vocabulary, the book will facilitate more effective communication between biologists and AI tool developers.




1. Balasubramanian, H., Hobson, C. M., Chew, T.-L. & Aaron, J. S. Imagining the future of optical microscopy: Everything, everywhere, all at once. Communications Biology 6, 1096 (2023).


2. Wait, E. C., Reiche, M. A. & Chew, T.-L. Hypothesis-driven quantitative fluorescence microscopy – the importance of reverse-thinking in experimental design. Journal of Cell Science 133, jcs250027 (2020).


3. Lee, R. M., Eisenman, L. R., Khuon, S., Aaron, J. S. & Chew, T.-L. Believing is seeing – the deceptive influence of bias in quantitative microscopy. Journal of Cell Science 137, jcs261567 (2024).

title: 2  AI in a Nutshell
text:
2.1 What is Artificial Intelligence?
Empirical science relies on the analysis and interpretation of large amounts of diverse raw data. In the life sciences, microscopy has become one of the largest sources of such data. A single light-sheet experiment can produce terabytes of volumetric time-lapse data; high-content screening campaigns image millions of cells across thousands of conditions; electron microscopy reconstructs tissue at nanometer-scale resolution across volumes approaching a cubic millimeter, yielding more than a petabyte of images from a single sample1,2.
A human expert might trace a few hundred neurons or label several thousand cells, but biological questions increasingly demand analysis that is both orders of magnitude larger and more complete. Even where each individual decision is easy, the sheer number of decisions puts manual analysis out of reach.
Artificial Intelligence (AI) methods promise to address this challenge, and they offer three distinct things. The first is speed: where a trained annotator might outline the cells in a hundred images per day, a well-designed AI model does the same in seconds, and many copies of it can run in parallel. The second is consistency: human observers vary in their judgments and tire over long sessions, whereas a model applies the same criteria uniformly. The third is sensitivity to structure that escapes human perception. Given only transmitted-light images, for instance, a model can predict where fluorescently labeled organelles would appear, reading information from an unstained sample as if it had been stained3.
But uniform is not the same as correct. Every AI method rests on two things: a computational structure that somebody designed and a set of examples it learned from. Choices on either side shape what the system does, and mistakes produce failures that are often distinctly non-human: systematic rather than sporadic, confident rather than hesitant, and capable of misleading a scientist in ways no tiring annotator would.
This chapter builds the vocabulary needed to make informed decisions: what terms like machine learning, deep learning, and supervised actually mean, what each family of methods asks of the user in return for what it does, and which failure modes each is prone to.
Two tasks recur here and throughout the book, because a great many microscopy applications reduce to one or the other: restoring images that the microscope could not record cleanly (Chapter 6), and segmenting them into the objects you want to measure (Chapter 9).
The term Artificial Intelligence has been attached to systems as different as a chess engine, a spam filter, and a chatbot. For someone choosing a method, the most useful thing that separates them is where the division of labor falls: which parts of the solution a person designs, and which parts the machine derives from data. In the seventy years since the term was coined4, that boundary has moved steadily in one direction—away from the designer and into the learned system. The three families below are stops along that path:
The three examples we started with have each moved along this path. Chess engines went from the hand-written evaluation rules of Deep Blue to the learned position estimates of today’s far stronger engines. Chatbots went from the scripted patterns of ELIZA to large language models. Spam filters went from keyword rules to learned word statistics and, increasingly, to large language models as well. The further along this path, the less of the solution you have to build—and the less of it you can inspect (Table 2.1).
The table shows a trend, not a law: a thousand-tree ensemble is no more readable than a small network. What changes reliably is how much of a system’s behavior you can anticipate without testing it. You know in advance that a threshold will break when the staining gets dimmer; a model that needed fewer examples gives no such warning. So prefer the earliest stop that solves your problem. Past that stop, trust has to be earned empirically, on ground truth the model never saw (Chapter 10). Much of what follows is about telling “works” from “mostly works”.

title: 2  AI in a Nutshell
text:
2.1 What is Artificial Intelligence?
The term Artificial Intelligence has been attached to systems as different as a chess engine, a spam filter, and a chatbot. For someone choosing a method, the most useful thing that separates them is where the division of labor falls: which parts of the solution a person designs, and which parts the machine derives from data. In the seventy years since the term was coined4, that boundary has moved steadily in one direction—away from the designer and into the learned system. The three families below are stops along that path:
Rule-based systems: you design everything. The quantities to measure, the algorithm that acts on them, and every parameter value are chosen by you, and you adjust them for a new sample. This class includes conversational systems like ELIZA5, expert systems for medical diagnosis like MYCIN6, web search ranked by PageRank7, the behavior of non-player characters in video games, image features designed to match views of the same scene across viewpoint changes8, and the thresholding, morphological operations, and watershed transforms that carried quantitative microscopy for decades9. Nothing about such a system is mysterious: every decision follows from a known rule, so a failure can be traced to the rule that produced it and repaired by editing that rule. The price is that an expert has to anticipate every scenario in advance, as well as design and test the rules to address each and every scenario.
Machine learning: you design the structure, and examples fix the parameters. Rather than defining everything, you specify a family of functions with free parameters and let an optimization procedure choose the parameters that reproduce the expected outcome on a set of examples. Classic methods learn only the decision, on top of hand-designed features. Support vector machines10, for example, learn to sort cells into classes from their measured size, shape, and brightness. Boosting trains a sequence of simple decision trees, each one correcting the errors its predecessors left behind11,12. This boosting technique can be used to score cell phenotypes in CellProfiler Analyst (Tip 7.1) and, when paired with box filters that can be computed extremely fast, can make face detection real-time13. Random forests instead train many trees independently, each on a random subset of the examples, and let them vote14. They drive interactive pixel classification in tools like ilastik15 (Chapter 8). Deep learning pushes the boundary one level deeper: the features themselves are learned, together with the decision that uses them (Section 2.1.1). The principle was demonstrated on handwritten digits in the 1990s16, but only in 2012, when labeled data and GPUs caught up, did it decisively outperform hand-designed pipelines on large-scale image recognition17.
What stays on the designer’s side is the architecture, the training objective, and the examples—annotated by hand, produced by a second measurement, as when one imaging modality is used to predict another3, or supplied by the data itself, as when a model learns to reconstruct image regions that were masked out18. Interpretability erodes along the same step. As long as the features are engineered, you can easily ask which measurement drove a call, because the measurements have names: area, eccentricity, mean intensity in the second channel. Once the features are learned, they do not trivially decompose into something a person would recognize. In practice, you find out what such a model does by watching what it does, although a growing body of interpretability research recovers a good deal of its reasoning (Section 2.4.3).
Foundation models: you use or adapt what somebody else has learned. These are machine learning models too; what sets them apart is scale and how you use them. A foundation model is pre-trained on an enormous collection of images or text, usually for a task that needs no annotation because the data supplies its own answers: predict the next word of a sentence, or fill in a masked-out patch of an image18. To do this well, the model has to learn how such data are structured in general. What it retains is a general-purpose representation, not the answer to any particular question, and with enough data this representation even replaces assumptions that designers used to build into the architecture19. Adapting the model to a real task reuses all of this instead of rebuilding it, whether by fine-tuning on a modest set of labeled examples or by training it to follow instructions20. That is why a problem that would otherwise demand tens of thousands of annotations can often be solved with a few hundred. A single pre-training run serves many different tasks. Segment Anything (SAM), for example, outlines structures it was never explicitly taught: objects you point to with a few clicks or a box21, mark once in a video to have them followed through every frame22, or simply name in a short phrase23.
The catch is that a model can only absorb the structure of the data it was trained on. Because those data are typically vast, proprietary, or both, its biases and gaps are inherited unseen. This is what can make foundation models wrong in ways that are hard to anticipate. How these models are pre-trained, adapted, and potentially misapplied is the subject of Section 2.2.2 and Chapter 3.
The three examples we started with have each moved along this path. Chess engines went from the hand-written evaluation rules of Deep Blue to the learned position estimates of today’s far stronger engines. Chatbots went from the scripted patterns of ELIZA to large language models. Spam filters went from keyword rules to learned word statistics and, increasingly, to large language models as well. The further along this path, the less of the solution you have to build—and the less of it you can inspect (Table 2.1).
Table 2.1: From left to right, more of the solution is derived from data, and it gets harder to find out why a system did what it did.

You know in advance that a threshold will break when the staining gets dimmer; a model that needed fewer examples gives no such warning. So prefer the earliest stop that solves your problem. Past that stop, trust has to be earned empirically, on ground truth the model never saw (Chapter 10). Much of what follows is about telling “works” from “mostly works”.

title: 2  AI in a Nutshell
text:
2.1.1 How deep learning learns
A deep learning model is one large function that turns an image into the desired output: a class, a mask, a restored image. It is built by chaining many simple steps: weighted sums of pixel values, small filters slid across the image, and simple operations such as setting negative values to zero. The weights in these steps are the model’s free parameters, often millions of them, and they start out random.
Training compares the model’s output with the expected one. A loss function turns the difference into a single number, the error. Every step of the model is differentiable, so for each parameter one can compute how a tiny change would change the error. The chain rule of calculus, applied backwards from the error through all steps (backpropagation), does this for all parameters at once, and gradient descent nudges each one a little in the direction that lowers the error. Repeated over many examples until the error stops falling, this process turns random parameters into a working model16. Because the whole chain from pixels to output is trained together, the model learns its own features rather than relying on measurements a person designed.
Such models are called artificial neural networks by historical analogy: many simple units, each adding up weighted inputs and passing the result through a simple threshold-like response, wired into a network whose collective behavior is far richer than any unit’s. “Deep” refers to the many layers of such units stacked on top of each other.
Differentiability is the only hard constraint, which leaves great freedom in how the steps are arranged. These architecture choices are where knowledge about the data re-enters a system that would otherwise have to learn everything from examples. Convolutional neural networks slide the same small filters across the whole image, building in the knowledge that a nucleus looks the same wherever it appears. Transformer architectures, originally developed for language, compare every part of the input with every other part, which helps when distant regions belong together—across a volume, or across the frames of a time-lapse. Chapter 4 explains architectures, loss functions, and the optimization procedures in detail.
The same freedom lets known physics be written into a model instead of learned from examples. If the point spread function of the microscope has been measured, the network does not have to rediscover how the microscope blurs: the known blur can be built into the architecture or the loss, and learning is spent only on what the optics do not explain24,25. Such physics-informed models often need fewer training images, can be trained on images simulated from the optics, and produce intermediate results with a physical meaning, such as an estimate of the unblurred specimen, which makes them easier to check. Chapter 6 develops them for deconvolution and aberration correction.

title: 2  AI in a Nutshell
text:
2.2 Learning from examples
The promise of machine learning is that it can infer the rules from examples. Two conditions have to hold:
The model must be able to represent and express the rules.
The examples must be enough to pin them down.
Both fail quietly. A model that sees image patches too small to contain a whole cell cannot learn anything that depends on cell shape or size, however many patches it is shown. A model shown only healthy cells cannot learn to recognize a diseased one. And the more a system has to discover for itself, the more examples it needs: learning a decision on top of a few well-chosen measurements takes fewer cells than learning what to measure in the first place.
The approaches below differ in where the training signal comes from: a person who annotated the data, the structure of the data itself, or the consequences of an action. This determines how much annotation you have to provide and what kind of answer you get back, but not, by itself, how accurate that answer is. It is also a separate question from the division of labor in Section 2.1: a deep learning model can be trained with labels or without them, and clustering, the classic method that needs no labels at all, works on hand-designed measurements as well as on learned ones.

title: 2  AI in a Nutshell
section: 2.2.1 Supervised learning: the answer is given
text:
2.2.1 Supervised learning: the answer is given
In supervised learning, every training image comes paired with the correct answer, the target, and the model learns to produce that answer from the image. The recipe does not care what the answer is: the same machinery classifies cells, outlines them, or predicts one channel from another. What changes is the form of the target, and in microscopy image analysis, that form varies a lot:
A category for an entire image or for one cell: treated or control, mitotic or interphase.
A position: a point per cell, or a box around it, saying where things are without saying where they end.
A class for every pixel—nucleus, cytoplasm, background—which is what semantic segmentation asks for26.
An identity for every object, so that two touching nuclei are two things rather than one region. This is instance segmentation, and it is what counting and per-cell measurements need.
Another image: a low-noise acquisition of the same field as the target for a noisy one27, or a fluorescence channel as the target for the transmitted-light image it is predicted from3.
The last case is still supervision, even though nobody annotated anything: the target came from a second measurement (Section 2.3.2).
The form of the target is the form of the answer you get back: a model trained on one class per image will never hand you cell boundaries, however many images it has seen. The target does not dictate how the model gets there, though. Instance segmentation in particular is rarely predicted directly: most methods predict something for every pixel, such as cell boundaries or the direction to each cell’s center, and assemble objects from it in a second step (Section 2.3.1).
Supervision has the virtue of directness. What you want the model to do is what the loss function measures, so accuracy can be quantified on labeled examples the model never saw, and a failure can at least be named: these nuclei were merged, those were missed. None of the label-free methods below offer that.
The cost is that the targets have to be made, usually by hand, and that they are not merely training material: they are the definition of the task. Systematic annotator habits become model behavior: if your annotators consistently skip dim nuclei at the edge of the field, so will the model, silently and everywhere. Where two experts disagree, the model learns the average of a disagreement rather than a fact, which sets a ceiling on any accuracy you can later claim. Curating such a set is the subject of Chapter 5.
How much annotation is involved varies over orders of magnitude, and two rules of thumb cover most of it. Adapting a pre-trained model to your data takes far fewer labels than training one from scratch (Chapter 9). And label shapes differ enormously in price: one class per image or one click per cell is quick; a dense mask of a crowded field is the most expensive annotation in routine use. When a count is all you need, buy the label shape that gives you counts.

title: 2  AI in a Nutshell
text:
2.2.2 Learning without labels
Two families of methods need no annotation at all. Without a person supplying the right answer, both scale to as much data as a microscope can generate, but neither can tell you whether what it found means anything biologically.
Unsupervised learning is the older and stricter of the two: it receives the images, or measurements derived from them, and nothing else. It optimizes a property of the data itself rather than agreement with a target: how compactly the data can be grouped, or how well a compressed version reproduces the original. Dimensionality reduction condenses the hundreds of numbers measured per cell into two or three, so that a whole screen fits into a scatter plot28. Clustering sorts the cells into groups without being told what the groups mean. Together they are the standard tools of morphological profiling, which measures many features on every cell in every well and looks for structure in the result29. Compounds with indistinguishable profiles then become candidates for a shared mechanism.
The limitation is easy to state and easy to forget: the algorithm separates points in the feature space it was given, and nothing guarantees that this space aligns with a biological category. Change the features and the groups change with them. The assumptions have moved from the labels into the features. A cluster is a hypothesis about your data; it becomes a finding only when independent evidence confirms it.
Self-supervised learning goes one step further: it turns unlabeled data into a supervised problem. The usual recipe is to withhold part of the data and train the model to restore it, for example masked patches of an image18 or masked words in a sentence30. Hiding single pixels of a noisy image and predicting them from their neighbors trains a denoiser that has never seen a clean image31. Movies are so redundant that a model still learns well when it has to fill in 90% or more of each clip32.
The task sounds circular, but it cannot be solved by simple statistics. Filling a large hole convincingly requires some idea of what put the pixels there: that a membrane continues where it is hidden, that nuclei have characteristic shapes and textures, that illumination varies smoothly across the field. A network trained this way at sufficient scale comes to represent much of the structure that generated its images, without ever being told what that structure is.
A self-supervised denoiser is trained for its output: the restored pixel is the product, and the representation is only a means to it (Chapter 6). In pre-training it is the other way around. The reconstruction is discarded, and the representation is what you keep. This also separates self-supervision from clustering: clustering hands you groups to interpret, whereas a representation is not yet an answer to anything. A second stage puts it to work. Fine-tuning on a few hundred annotated images can turn a generic visual representation into a segmentation model for your specimen, and semi-supervised training adds a large pool of unlabeled images to a small labeled set. Neither repeats the expensive pre-training. On ImageNet, a benchmark of more than a million labeled photographs, pre-training without labels and fine-tuning with 1% of them comes close to a network trained on all labels. That is a tenfold gain in label efficiency over earlier approaches33.
Not every general-purpose model got there without labels. The original Segment Anything model was trained on roughly a billion masks in eleven million images, masks that annotators produced with the help of the model itself. A dedicated component reads the clicks, boxes, or rough masks you give it21. The model segments structures it was never explicitly taught, but only in the ways its designers built in. Either way, the training data sets the limit: a model absorbs the structure of the images it was shown, with their biases and artifacts, not the structure of the world. Versions fine-tuned on microscopy data exist34,35, but whether they help on your images has to be tested. Chapter 9 covers how to fine-tune, and Chapter 10 how to tell whether it worked.
TipOther recipes for self-supervision
Filling in masked-out data are only the most direct recipe. A second family learns embeddings that are insensitive to irrelevant variation but expressive enough to distinguishing meaningful classes. A contrastive loss pulls together the embeddings of two altered versions of the same image and pushes apart those of different images36; other methods only ask the network to agree with a slowly updated copy of itself37. Text models learn embeddings too, so that passages about the same topic land close together30,38.
The result can be more structured than the training task suggests: the image regions such a network attends to trace the outlines of objects, although nothing in the training asked for a segmentation37. Trained on large, carefully curated image collections, these networks learn features general enough that many tasks need only a simple classifier on top39,40.
A third recipe hides part of the input, as in reconstruction, but asks the network to predict the representation of the hidden part rather than its pixels, because fine detail is largely unpredictable and not worth reproducing41.
Recipes that only reward agreement share a trap: describing every image the same way satisfies them perfectly and learns nothing. Most methods guard against this collapse with an assortment of engineering tricks; recent work replaces them with the single requirement that the embeddings be spread out evenly in all directions42.
NoteClustering or segmentation? Let the question decide
Take one compound screen: a few thousand fields, three channels, a few hundred conditions. Two questions a biologist might reasonably ask of it need entirely different methods.
How many cells are dying in each condition? The category already exists—you can say what a dying cell looks like—and the answer is a number per condition, so every cell has to be found and judged: supervised detection or segmentation, then supervised classification. You provide annotations, and what you get back is a measurement, a count you can put an error bar on, because annotated images the model never saw tell you how many cells it missed or invented.
Are there phenotypes in this screen I have not thought of? Here there is nothing to supervise, because naming the classes is the result you are after. So you measure many features per cell and group the cells, or whole conditions, whose measurements look alike. Without annotation, you get a hypothesis: a set of conditions that behave similarly, which needs an independent experiment before it counts as a finding.
The rule generalizes. Supervised methods answer questions you can already phrase; label-free methods help you find the question. Many projects run the second kind of analysis once, to decide what is worth counting, and the first kind forever after.
The two also combine more often than they compete: the features are usually measured on cells that a segmentation model found first, so an exploratory analysis inherits every bias of that model—a reason to check the segmentation even when the result is only a hypothesis.

title: 2  AI in a Nutshell
text:
2.2.3 Learning from consequences: reinforcement learning
A third approach needs no examples at all. In reinforcement learning, an agent acts, the environment responds, and a reward scores how well that went; the agent adjusts its behavior to collect more reward, generating its own training data as it goes43. The reward can be sparse and arrive late—a game won twenty moves after the decisive one—which is what makes the approach both powerful and expensive.
Image analysis gives it little to work with, because there is no action to take on an image that has already been recorded: the pixels do not respond. Microscopy does offer one natural fit, and it is at the instrument. In closed-loop acquisition the model chooses where to look next, at what magnification, and for how long, and those choices have consequences that can be scored—an event captured or missed, a sample bleached or spared. Chapter 7 takes up event-driven imaging.
The term will also be familiar from large language models, which use reinforcement learning from human feedback. This is the stage in which a language model is tuned toward responses that people rated highly20. The mechanics are the same, with a learned stand-in for human preference supplying the reward (Chapter 3).

title: 2  AI in a Nutshell
text:
2.3 The Tasks
The approaches above sort methods by where their training signal comes from; the tasks below sort them by what comes out.

title: 2  AI in a Nutshell
text:
2.3.1 Segmentation: turning pixels into objects
Segmentation converts an image into a list of things you can measure. Counts, sizes, per-cell intensities, colocalization, morphology—almost every quantitative claim made from a microscopy image passes through it, which is why the rest of this book keeps returning to it.
The literature uses three terms, not always consistently. Semantic segmentation assigns each pixel a class without separating objects of the same class, instance segmentation gives each object its own identity (Section 2.2.1), and panoptic segmentation does both at once. Tip 8.2 works the distinction through on a real image.
What makes an annotation expensive is not the number of pixels but how precisely the shape has to be drawn. Semantic segmentation is forgiving: a pixel classifier can be trained from a few brush strokes per class on a handful of images, as interactive tools such as ilastik have done since before deep learning15. Instance segmentation is not, because every object needs its own identity, and most methods need each boundary drawn accurately—slow, careful work rather than a lot of clicking.
How much of that care is genuinely necessary depends on the method rather than the task. A network that predicts an embedding per pixel needs the pixels of one object to agree, not its boundary to be right, so in principle sparse labels should suffice, even though published implementations often use dense ones44,45. A network that only has to place a box needs no outlines at all, which is why annotating for counting is cheap. What cannot be negotiated is the number of dimensions: a 3D annotation has to stay consistent from section to section, so it is one decision carried through a volume rather than one drawing per slice, and adding time compounds it again.
How a segmentation is produced is rarely what the label suggests. Object identity has no canonical output: which integer a given cell receives is arbitrary, and swapping two of them changes nothing about the answer, so there is nothing stable for a per-pixel classifier to predict. Almost every method therefore predicts a quantity that is well defined per pixel and assembles objects from it in a second step.
TipA deeper understanding of what segmentation methods actually predict
Methods differ mainly in what the network is asked to output per pixel, and each choice implies its own way of recovering objects.
Boundaries and affinities. The network predicts, for each pair of neighboring pixels, whether they belong to the same object46. Objects are then grown by watershed, or by agglomerative merging. Including pairs that are farther apart than one pixel helps detect thin gaps and provides evidence that two pixels belong to different objects; the mutex watershed uses that evidence to separate objects without seed points or a threshold47,48.
A description of the shape the pixel belongs to. StarDist predicts the distance from each pixel to the object’s edge in a fixed set of directions and keeps the best non-overlapping polygons49. Local shape descriptors predict summary statistics of the surrounding object—its size, elongation, and offset to its center—as an additional training target that markedly improves the affinities predicted alongside50. PatchPerPix goes furthest and predicts an entire small binary mask of the object around each pixel, then assembles objects from the patches that agree51.
A direction toward the object’s center. Cellpose predicts, for every pixel, the direction toward the center of its cell. Following these directions makes the pixels of one cell converge on a single point, and those that arrive together become an object52. Nothing here assumes a shape, which is why it copes with irregular and elongated cells.
An embedding per pixel. The network learns a vector that should be identical for pixels of the same object and different across objects, and the objects fall out by clustering44,45.
One object at a time. Flood-filling networks start from a seed and iteratively extend a single mask until it stops growing, then move on to the next seed53. This sidesteps the identity problem rather than solving it, and it has proven itself where objects are enormous and branching, as in reconstructing neurons from electron microscopy.
The grouping step deserves as much attention as the network. It is where most false splits and false merges are made, and where most of the parameters a user still has to set actually live. It is also the knob that trades the two errors against each other, and which one you want depends on the question. A false split, or one cell cut in two, is usually easier to see and quicker to repair than a false merge, especially in objects with complicated shapes. Moreover, a merge quietly averages two cells into one measurement.
Chapter 4 covers the architectures behind these predictions, Chapter 8 how to find a tool that already makes them, Chapter 9 how to train or fine-tune one on your own data, and Chapter 10 how to tell whether it worked.

title: 2  AI in a Nutshell
section: 2.3.2 Restoration: recovering what the microscope could not record
text:
2.3.2 Restoration: recovering what the microscope could not record
Every image is a degraded observation. The microscope blurs the specimen by its point spread function, the detector records a finite number of photons and so returns a noisy count, and the pixel grid is often coarser than the finest detail you would like to resolve. Restoration estimates the underlying signal from what was recorded. This is an ill-posed inverse problem, because many different specimens are consistent with the same recorded image.
Supervised restoration fits the template of Section 2.2.1 exactly, with an image as the target instead of a label. The kind of target image defines the task: a high-signal acquisition of the same field for denoising, a sharper one for deconvolution and aberration correction, a higher-resolution or differently acquired one for resolution enhancement. Chapter 6 develops all of these. Restoration can also use a different channel entirely as a target for modality translation, where a fluorescence signal is predicted from transmitted light3.
The reason to care is not that the images look better. Noise, blur, and limited resolution are all paid for in photons, and photons are what a living sample cannot spare. A denoiser that recovers a usable image from a tenth of the illumination converts directly into a tenth of the phototoxicity, or ten times the frame rate, or a time-lapse that runs ten times longer before the specimen gives out. Restoration is an acquisition technique that happens to run after acquisition.
One caveat matters enormously: restoration is not measurement. Wherever the recorded data carry too little information, the estimate comes from the training set rather than from the specimen. Section 2.3.4 names the mechanism and Chapter 6 collects the consequences.
Denoising often does not need a clean reference: self-supervision (Section 2.2.2) can train a denoiser on noisy images alone.
TipDenoising without a clean image
Deep-learning-based denoising methods rest on one asymmetry: the signal in an image is predictable from its surroundings, and the noise, by definition, is not. Put a network in a position where it can only reproduce the predictable part, and it denoises.
The direct approach needs a pair of images of the same field, one noisy and one with high signal, and learns the map between them27. Acquiring that pair is easy on a fixed sample and often impossible on a living one, which moves and changes between exposures.
Noise2Noise drops the need for a high-signal image. Two independent noisy exposures of the same field are enough, because the network cannot predict the particular noise in the target from the noise in the input; the best it can do is the signal the two share54.
Noise2Void drops the need for a pair. A single noisy image suffices: hide one pixel, ask the network to predict it from its neighbors, repeat31. The network never sees the value it is trying to reproduce, so it cannot copy the noise. What it does require is that the noise be independent between pixels—true of photon shot noise, false of line artifacts such as scanning stripes, where the fix is to hide whole lines instead of single pixels55.
A noisy image is consistent with many clean ones, and a network trained to minimize the average squared error returns their blend. Diversity denoising instead learns the distribution of clean images consistent with the input and draws samples from it, making the ambiguity visible rather than smoothing it away56. It is a generative model in the sense of Section 2.3.4.
Similar networks can also undo a deliberate mix. If two labeled structures are imaged into a single channel, a network trained on separately acquired examples of each can pull them apart again, so fewer channels have to be acquired in the first place57.
One assumption is shared by all of them: whatever cannot be predicted is treated as noise. Structure that is genuinely rare and genuinely unpredictable is therefore exactly what they are most likely to erase.
Chapter 6 discusses these approaches in more detail.

title: 2  AI in a Nutshell
text:
2.3.3 Classification, detection, and tracking
Classification attaches one label to an image, or to an object already found in it: cell type, cell cycle stage, treated or control, healthy or diseased. Image-level labels are the cheapest annotation there is, which makes classification a quick way to find out whether a signal is present in your data at all.
Detection locates each object by a point or a box, but not its exact outline. That annotation is dramatically simpler than a detailed boundary mask, and the output is sufficient whenever the answer is a count, a position, or a trigger to act on (Chapter 7).
Tracking links objects across frames, which is where much of the interesting biology is—division, migration, differentiation, events that a single timepoint cannot show. It combines two problems: finding the objects in each frame, which is segmentation or detection as above, and association, deciding which object in this frame is which object in the next.
Cell division makes it harder than plain matching, because one object legitimately becomes two, so the answer is a lineage tree rather than a set of paths—and a dividing cell rounds up and changes appearance precisely when the association is most delicate. Association errors also compound, since a single swap corrupts every measurement downstream of it in that lineage. A method can therefore score well on the fraction of correct links and still recover almost no complete tracks58, which is why tracking has no single accuracy number (Chapter 10).
TipHow tracking is actually done
Most trackers in use separate the two problems: segment or detect each frame independently, then link. The separation is convenient, because either part can be replaced independently. It is also the structure that most standard benchmarks assume58.
The classical linker has not been displaced. Linear assignment solves frame-to-frame matching as an optimal assignment problem, then makes a second global pass that stitches track fragments together and repairs gaps, merges, and splits59. This is the main engine inside TrackMate, the tool most microscopists will actually open, which now accepts modern segmentation models as its detector60. An important finding from a decade of benchmarking is that segmentation quality dominates: a simple linker on good detections beats a sophisticated linker on poor ones58.
Deep learning has changed the linker in three ways. It can learn the association itself, with a transformer scoring candidate matches from position and appearance across a window of frames, which works across bacteria, cell culture, and particles without per-dataset tuning61. It can fold detection and linking into one network, predicting for each pixel the offset to where its object was in the previous frame62. Or it can supply many candidate segmentations, from several models and parameter settings, and leave it to temporal consistency to choose among them, which is what makes terabyte-scale embryo recordings tractable63. Video foundation models are an obvious candidate as well: SAM 2 carries a mask through a video without any retraining22, and microscopy time-lapses are videos too.
What remains hard is well documented. Pre-trained trackers generalize poorly to morphologies and modalities they have not seen; densely annotated, fully tracked datasets are scarce, which limits what more supervision can fix; and recovery of complete lineages lags well behind the local link-accuracy scores that are usually reported58.
Rare-event detection uses these tasks to find the one cell in ten thousand that does something interesting. A model can search vast amounts of recorded data for such events, and if it runs fast enough, it can steer the microscope during acquisition: record the event in detail while it happens, and spare the sample and the storage during the hours in which nothing happens (Chapter 7). The two kinds of error weigh very differently. A false negative is a lost event, and when events are this rare, every one counts. A false positive costs less, but even a low rate adds up: one false alarm per thousand cells buries each real event under ten false ones. That is acceptable, because the detector does not have to be the last word. Tuned to miss as little as possible, it shrinks the pile enough that a slower, more accurate method, or a person, can sort through what remains.

title: 2  AI in a Nutshell
section: 2.3.4 Generative models: sampling instead of averaging
text:
2.3.4 Generative models: sampling instead of averaging
A model trained to minimize the average squared error returns the mean of all outcomes consistent with its input. Where the input is ambiguous, that mean is a blend, which is why strongly denoised images can look slightly waxy. A generative model is instead trained to draw samples from the distribution of possible outcomes. Each sample carries the texture and edge contrast of real data, and running the model twice on the same input yields two different answers. No single sample represents the whole distribution, though: it is one plausible answer, not the best estimate.
Four families are in current use. Variational autoencoders compress an image into a small code and decode it back; because the code is a distribution rather than a single point, sampling it yields different plausible reconstructions64. Adversarial training pits the generator against a second network that tries to tell generated images from real ones65. Diffusion models learn to reverse a gradual corruption by noise, and generate by denoising pure noise in many small steps66. Flow matching learns a more direct path from noise to data, which takes fewer steps67.
The risk follows from what sampling means: a generative model is built to produce output indistinguishable from real data, whether or not the input supports the particular detail it draws—a vesicle that is sharp, plausible, correctly textured, and never measured. This inverts the usual relation between image quality and trust: the restored image is more convincing than the raw data, so judging it by eye selects for exactly the failures you need to catch68. A structure that appears only after restoration must never be quantified.

title: 2  AI in a Nutshell
section: 2.4 Why It Fails, and How you find out
text: 2.4 Why It Fails, and How you find out

title: 2  AI in a Nutshell
section: 2.4.1 Overfitting and the discipline of splitting data
text:
2.4.1 Overfitting and the discipline of splitting data
It is easy to say what kind of label, field of view, or resolution a task requires, and much harder to know whether a set of examples is sufficient, because nobody knows in advance which rules the model has to infer. Worse, the model may find a shortcut that works perfectly on the training examples and fails on the intended task. The only way to find out is to measure performance on a separate test dataset that was never used for training.
There is a second problem: gradient descent keeps driving the training loss lower, eventually by memorizing the training examples rather than learning rules that generalize. Because no training set fully represents the real world, this overfitting sets in if training runs long enough and the model sees each example too often. So when do you stop?
The answer is a validation dataset: examples withheld from training but used to monitor performance along the way. When performance on them stops improving, training stops.
The validation set must stay separate from the test set. Validation examples are not used for gradient descent, but they still shape the final model: you pick the training iteration, architecture, or hyperparameters that do best on them, so the model can overfit to the validation set too. Only the test set, used once at the very end, gives an unbiased estimate of performance on new data from the same source.
Both splits only work if the withheld examples are genuinely separate. Neighboring patches from the same stack are nearly identical, so splitting patches at random scatters near-copies across all three sets, and the score that comes back measures memory rather than performance. Chapter 5 covers how to build and split a dataset in practice, Chapter 10 what to measure on it.

title: 2  AI in a Nutshell
text:
2.4.2 Domain shift and shortcut learning
A model can pass both checks and still do worse on images acquired a few months later. Training and test data came from the same experiment; the new images did not. This is domain shift. The causes are mundane: a different objective, a realigned laser, a new batch of mounting medium, the same cell line at a higher passage number. The result is rarely outright failure but a slow degradation: slightly worse masks, a few more missed cells, a shifted effect size.
Microscopy is more exposed to this than most of computer vision. A model trained on hundreds of millions of photographs has already seen most of the variation it will meet. A microscopy model often knows only one laboratory’s protocol on one instrument, and that protocol changes routinely, sometimes without anyone noticing.
The same narrowness allows a second failure. One experiment’s images cannot separate the regularities of the biology from those of the protocol. If something incidental correlates with the label, gradient descent will use it, because it optimizes the loss and not the biology. This is shortcut learning69. The outer wells of a plate lose more medium to evaporation, and their cells look different70, so a classifier whose controls sit in column 1 may be reading well position rather than phenotype. Shortcuts need not come from the sample at all. Training crops that are mostly background teach a segmentation model to predict background everywhere, which minimizes the loss and finds nothing (Section 8.6.2).
Neither failure shows up as a poor validation score, because the validation data share the protocol, and therefore the confounds, of the training data. For example, in one case, it was easier to train a model to identify the hospital and department that acquired an image than one that would successfully classify pneumonia in images from other hospitals71.
Split at the level of whatever will vary in practice: whole plates, whole sessions, whole cell lines, not random crops from a common pool. That does not prevent domain shift, but it makes it visible before you rely on the model. The rest belongs elsewhere: a training set that spans the variation you expect, and augmentation to extend it (Chapter 5); fine-tuning when a published model does not transfer (Chapter 9); and appropriate measures of success (Chapter 10). A reported accuracy describes the data it was measured on, and says little about yours72.

title: 2  AI in a Nutshell
section: 2.4.3 The black box: a correct answer is not an explanation
text:
2.4.3 The black box: a correct answer is not an explanation
Nothing inside a trained network is hidden: every weight and every intermediate value can be printed. But the resulting features do not trivially decompose into interpretable quantities (Section 2.1). That is what the black box is: not secrecy, but the absence of any description of the model short enough to reason with.
This has two important consequences. The first is that behavior cannot be predicted by inspection. For a rule-based pipeline, you can read off where it will fail, because the rules are written down; for a network, the failures of Section 2.4.1 and Section 2.4.2 can only be found by measurement. The second is that a correct prediction carries no reason with it. A classifier may separate treated cells from controls on every plate for something other than the phenotype, and no held-out test will reveal it, because the prediction is not wrong. That the network distinguishes the conditions is a measurement; that the treatment changes mitochondrial morphology is a claim the network never made.
The confidence score the model reports is not a check on this. It comes out of the same computation as the prediction, and current networks routinely report confidence above their measured accuracy73, and most severely under domain shift, exactly when a warning would be most useful74. Whether a given score can be trusted is itself measurable (Chapter 10).
What remains is evaluation on data like yours, and interpretability methods that have themselves been tested. A common tool is an attribution map, a per-pixel image of how much each part of the input contributed to the output; several widely used variants produce nearly the same map after the network’s weights are randomized, so they were never reporting on the trained model at all75. Methods that pass such checks can deliver. A network trained on electron micrographs identifies which of six neurotransmitters a Drosophila synapse releases in 87% of cases. Ordinary attribution maps did not reveal what it relied on, but comparing each synapse with a generated counterfactual, the same synapse made to look like another transmitter type, isolated ultrastructural differences a person could name and nobody had described before76.
A network nobody can explain can still be a good instrument, provided it has been characterized like one.

title: 2  AI in a Nutshell
text:
2.5 What comes next
A model can be put to two uses. In measurement, you already know what to count and the model counts it. It is part of the instrument, and its output is a number in your results77. In exploration, you do not yet know what to look for, and the output is a suggestion about what to measure next. The two are not separate methods: the same segmentation model can count the phenotype you asked for and then reveal one you did not. What matters is saying which you were doing.
Using a model as an instrument means characterizing it like one: an accuracy, the metric it was computed with, and the data it was measured on. The last is the easiest to leave out and the most important (Section 2.4.2). The model, its version, whether you fine-tuned it and on what, and the score on held-out data belong in the methods, as specifically as an objective or an exposure time.
The rest of the book takes up what this chapter has only named. Chapter 3 covers the models whose output is language, Chapter 4 architectures and loss functions, and Chapter 5 the examples everything depends on. Chapter 6 treats restoration in depth, and Chapter 7 models that act on the specimen instead of reporting on it. Chapter 8 helps you find an existing tool, Chapter 9 shows how to train or fine-tune one, Chapter 10 how to measure whether it worked, and Chapter 11 where exploration is already producing new biology.

title: 3  Large Language Models and AI Agents
text:
3.1 From Deep Learning to Foundation Models and Generative AI
Over the past decade, the way we analyze microscopy data has changed markedly. What began with specialized deep learning models for individual tasks — segmentation, denoising, classification — has evolved into a broader landscape where artificial intelligence (AI) systems can assist with experiment planning, code generation, instrument control, and workflow adaptation. This chapter traces that evolution and equips microscopists with the knowledge to navigate it.
We begin by examining the limitations of traditional deep learning and the rise of foundation models that generalize across imaging modalities. We then introduce Large Language Models and explain how they work at an intuitive level (Section 3.2), before exploring how function calling transformed them from text generators into action-taking agents (Section 3.3). The chapter covers vision-language models for microscopy (Section 3.4) and the growing ecosystem of AI agents that can orchestrate complex workflows, control instruments, and generate software on demand (Section 3.5, Section 3.6). A hands-on practical guide (Section 3.7) provides concrete workflows for getting started, followed by an honest discussion of challenges, implications for the profession, and an outlook on where the field is headed (Section 3.8).
Throughout, we maintain a critical perspective: these tools offer genuine capabilities, but they also hallucinate, carry biases, and cannot replace the domain expertise of trained microscopists. Understanding both the power and the limitations is essential for responsible adoption.
The application of AI to microscopy has changed rapidly. The modern era began with convolutional neural networks (CNNs), which improved how we process biological images. These supervised models were trained to perform specific tasks: classifying images, segmenting structures, denoising acquisitions, or translating between imaging modalities. Architectures like ResNet (for image classification) and U-Net (for segmentation and image-to-image translation) became foundational not only in bioimaging but across computer vision more broadly. See Chapter 4 for a detailed discussion of these architectures.

title: 3  Large Language Models and AI Agents
section: 3.1.1 The Extrapolation Problem: Why Task-Specific Models Break Down
text:
3.1.1 The Extrapolation Problem: Why Task-Specific Models Break Down
These early deep learning approaches showed impressive capabilities within their training domains, but they carry a fundamental and often underappreciated limitation: neural networks are sophisticated pattern-matching systems that work reliably only when processing inputs similar to their training data (see Chapter 5). They are poor at extrapolation. A network trained to segment fluorescent nuclei in one cell line, imaged on one microscope, at one magnification, may fail — sometimes silently — when applied to a different cell type, a different microscope, or even a different staining protocol. This brittleness has been documented systematically: standard neural networks fail at tasks as simple as arithmetic when tested outside their training range1, and the problem compounds for the complex, high-dimensional data typical of microscopy.
To illustrate this, we conducted a simple experiment (see the Python code) where we trained a multi-layer perceptron to learn addition using numbers in the range [-1,1]. When tested on progressively larger ranges, the model’s performance degrades severely — with errors increasing by approximately 7,700× from the training range (Figure 3.1).
Figure 3.1: Neural network extrapolation failure in simple addition. A standard MLP trained on the range [-1,1] shows severe performance degradation on larger number ranges, despite addition being a simple operation that should generalize perfectly. This illustrates the core limitation of neural networks as pattern-matching systems that fail outside their training distribution.
Figure 3.2 demonstrates the same problem with direct relevance to microscopy. When we apply a standard ResNet50 model trained on ImageNet to a natural photograph, it correctly identifies a cat with reasonable confidence. But when presented with a fluorescence microscopy image showing TRAP1 protein localization in human cells, the same model produces confident yet completely irrelevant predictions — “jellyfish” (36.2%), “velvet” (13.1%), “coral reef” (8.3%). The model has never encountered microscopy data, so it maps unfamiliar visual patterns onto the closest categories it knows.
Figure 3.2: Domain mismatch between natural and microscopy images. A ResNet50 model trained on ImageNet correctly classifies a cat photograph (left) but produces confident, irrelevant predictions for a TRAP1 protein immunofluorescence image (right). Image credit: Human Protein Atlas (https://www.proteinatlas.org/ENSG00000126602-TRAP1).
A researcher unfamiliar with the model’s training background might trust these confident predictions, potentially misinterpreting biological data. The 36.2% confidence in “jellyfish” illustrates a general failure mode: neural networks can produce authoritative-sounding but scientifically meaningless or misleading outputs when applied outside their intended domain. Stretching these models beyond their training distribution can result in hallucinated objects, irrelevant labels assigned with deceptively high confidence, or artifacts that mislead biological interpretation.
This does not mean that ImageNet-pretrained models are useless for microscopy — in practice, most deep learning approaches in bioimaging start from ImageNet-pretrained weights and then fine-tune on domain-specific data. But even after fine-tuning, the base model retains learned features from its original training. When the model encounters microscopy images with visual patterns that happen to resemble natural objects — jellyfish-like fluorescent textures, coral-like tissue structures — these embedded representations can influence predictions, potentially introducing systematic biases.

title: 3  Large Language Models and AI Agents
section: 3.1.2 The Rise of Generalist and Foundation Models
text:
3.1.2 The Rise of Generalist and Foundation Models
A major trend in bioimage analysis has been the shift from narrow, task-specific models toward generalist and foundation models that work across diverse imaging conditions without retraining.
Cellpose pioneered this approach for cell segmentation. By training on a diverse dataset spanning fluorescence, brightfield, and even non-microscopy images with similar visual characteristics, Cellpose achieved strong generalization across cell types and imaging modalities that previous models required separate training for. Cellpose 32 further advanced this by introducing one-click image restoration that enables segmentation even of degraded images — noisy, blurry, or undersampled data that would defeat earlier models.
Segment Anything Model (SAM), released by Meta in 2023, advanced the field of promptable segmentation further. Trained on over one billion masks from 11 million images, SAM demonstrated that a single model could segment essentially any object in any image through simple prompts (points, boxes, or text). Despite being trained entirely on natural images, SAM showed unexpected capability on out-of-domain scientific images, sparking a wave of microscopy-specific adaptations:
micro-SAM3 fine-tuned SAM specifically for light and electron microscopy, extending it to support 3D segmentation and cell tracking. micro-SAM provides interactive segmentation tools through a napari plugin, making foundation model capabilities directly accessible to microscopists.
CellSAM4 combined SAM with a custom cell detection module (CellFinder) to achieve expert-level segmentation performance across mammalian cells, yeast, and bacteria — all with a single unified model.
Cellpose-SAM5 adapted SAM’s pretrained transformer backbone to the Cellpose framework, achieving what the authors describe as superhuman generalization for cellular segmentation across diverse imaging conditions.
The key insight is that models trained on vast, diverse datasets can learn transferable visual features that generalize well to microscopy. A model that has processed billions of natural images learns representations of edges, textures, boundaries, and object structure that transfer effectively, even to fluorescent cells it has never encountered. This is the same principle underlying transfer learning, but operating at a much larger scale. See Section 9.2.6 for more information.
While these generalist models have made deep learning safer and more accessible, they remain largely focused on segmentation — a relatively well-defined computational task. More complex microscopy challenges such as classification across diverse experimental conditions, image restoration, spectral unmixing, or artificial labeling still require task-specific approaches. The gap between what generalist models can do and what microscopy research demands is precisely the space that Large Language Models and AI agents are beginning to fill.

title: 3  Large Language Models and AI Agents
text:
3.1.3 The Complexity Challenge
Microscopy presents complexity well beyond segmentation. Researchers routinely work with diverse labeling schemes, varying numbers of channels, different spatial scales, temporal dimensions, and countless combinations of experimental conditions. These multifaceted combinations make it difficult to build generalist models for broader tasks, and as a result, the vast majority of models remain highly task- and data-specific. This proliferation has driven community efforts such as the BioImage Model Zoo (https://bioimage.io) — a collaborative initiative to facilitate sharing of AI models across input image types and architectures, providing essential infrastructure for the community (Figure 3.3).
Figure 3.3: The BioImage Model Zoo serves as a centralized repository promoting FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) principles for AI models in bioimage analysis. The platform integrates with popular tools including ilastik, Fiji/ImageJ, QuPath, napari, and others, allowing researchers to access AI models through familiar interfaces.
Yet the growing ecosystem has also revealed an accessibility paradox. Model developers struggle with diverse training data requirements, validation protocols, and framework compatibility, while the burden of creating user-friendly interfaces often exceeds available time. Users face the opposite problem: an overwhelming array of model choices without clear guidance on which to select, complex software installations, and limited technical expertise to validate whether a model works on their specific data. As highlighted by Ouyang et al.6, the traditional desktop-centric paradigm — where analysis occurs in isolation on a single workstation — creates barriers to collaboration and reproducibility. While AI capabilities have advanced considerably, the practical barriers to using these tools have in many cases increased, widening the gap between AI potential and real-world adoption in biological research.
Modern microscopy data volumes amplify these challenges further. Terabytes of high-resolution images from time-lapse experiments, multi-channel fluorescence imaging, and high-content screening assays require sophisticated visualization and extensive manual interaction. Many important patterns, subtle phenotypes, or rare events are simply missed due to practical limitations of human-driven exploration. As following sections will highlight, agentic AI represents a potentially transformative tool to overcome some of these limitations.

title: 3  Large Language Models and AI Agents
section: 3.1.5 The Path Forward: From Generative AI to AI Agents
text:
3.1.5 The Path Forward: From Generative AI to AI Agents
Large language Models (LLMs) — such as those from OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic — interact through natural language rather than specialized interfaces. They can generate code, provide explanations, and execute actions through conversation, lowering many of the technical barriers that have limited AI adoption in microscopy.
A critical development was the introduction of function calling (also called tool use) — the ability for LLMs to invoke external tools, APIs (application programming interface), and software through structured interfaces rather than generating plain text. First introduced by OpenAI in June 2023, function calling transformed LLMs from text generators into systems that can execute code, query databases, control instruments, and interact with scientific software. Combined with standardized protocols like Anthropic’s Model Context Protocol (MCP, announced November 2024), this created a general-purpose interface layer connecting AI reasoning to existing scientific tools.
With tool-calling capabilities, LLMs can operate as AI agents — systems that plan actions, execute them, observe outcomes, and adapt iteratively. For bioimaging, this means AI agents can help select analysis methods, configure parameters, generate custom code, and troubleshoot failures through natural language interactions. Multimodal language models can also interpret microscopy images directly, combining visual understanding with code generation in a single interface. However, as we discuss throughout this chapter, these capabilities come with important limitations requiring careful human oversight.
The following sections explore each of these developments: how LLMs work (Section 3.2), how function calling enables tool use (Section 3.3), how vision-language models handle microscopy images (Section 3.4), and how AI agents are reshaping experimental workflows (Section 3.5, Section 3.6).

title: 3  Large Language Models and AI Agents
section: 3.2 Foundations of Large Language Models: An Intuitive Primer
text:
3.2 Foundations of Large Language Models: An Intuitive Primer
At its core, a Large Language Model (LLM) like ChatGPT, Gemini, or Claude is a text prediction engine operating at enormous scale. Its fundamental task is: given a sequence of text, predict the most probable next word. The autocomplete feature on your phone does something similar, but an LLM applies this principle with billions of parameters trained on a substantial fraction of human-written text. By repeatedly predicting the next word, an LLM can generate fluent, coherent paragraphs — and in the process, exhibit capabilities that go well beyond simple text completion, including code generation, logical reasoning, and scientific explanation.
crumbs: 3  Large Language Models and AI Agents

title: 3  Large Language Models and AI Agents
section: 3.2.1 How LLMs Learn: Training on the World’s Text
text:
3.2.1 How LLMs Learn: Training on the World’s Text
The “Large” in LLM refers to two aspects: the size of the neural network (with billions of adjustable parameters) and the volume of text it learns from. Training involves feeding the model a massive dataset comprising a significant portion of the public internet, digital books, scientific articles, and code repositories.
The training objective is conceptually straightforward: given a sequence of text, the model learns to predict the next word. For example, given the partial sentence “The scientist placed the sample on the microscope,” the model learns that “stage” is a likely next word. Before training, predictions are essentially random, but through billions of examples, the model gradually learns which words tend to follow which, adjusting its internal connections to improve predictions (see Chapter 4 for more details on the mechanics of training).
To process text, the model first breaks sentences into tokens — chunks that may be whole words or subword pieces. For instance, “microscope” might be a single token, while “fluorescence” might be split into “fluor” + “escence.” Each token is converted into a numerical vector through a process called embedding, creating a mathematical representation that captures meaning and context. These vectors pass through layers of the neural network, where the model learns how words relate to each other. After training on billions of sentences, the model develops a rich statistical map of language — the relationships between words, phrases, and concepts.
crumbs: 3  Large Language Models and AI Agents

title: 3  Large Language Models and AI Agents
section: 3.2.2 The Transformer: A Revolution in Understanding Context
text:
3.2.2 The Transformer: A Revolution in Understanding Context
The critical breakthrough enabling modern LLMs is the transformer architecture, introduced by Vaswani et al7. in 2017. Before this innovation, language models had very short “memory” and would lose track of context in longer text. The transformer introduced a mechanism called self-attention, which allows the model to weigh the importance of every word in the input simultaneously, regardless of position. When processing the sentence “The cell was stained with DAPI, which binds to DNA in the nucleus,” the attention mechanism enables the model to connect “nucleus” to “cell,” maintaining long-range context and generating coherent, relevant responses.

section: 3.2.4 Code Generation for Microscopy: Capabilities and Limits
text:
3.2.4 Code Generation for Microscopy: Capabilities and Limits
For bioimage analysis, LLM code generation is most valuable when it bridges the gap between a researcher who understands what analysis they need and the programming required to implement it. A microscopist who knows they need to measure nuclear fluorescence intensity across treatment conditions can describe this to an LLM and receive a working Python script — without memorizing the syntax for loading TIFF files or calling scikit-image functions. This lowers the barrier to computational analysis, particularly for researchers who understand the biology but lack extensive programming backgrounds.
How well does this actually work? A rigorous benchmark by Haase et. al.9 evaluated 18 LLMs on 57 bioimage analysis coding tasks with unit tests. The best-performing model (Claude 3.5 Sonnet) achieved a 58% pass rate, followed by GPT-4o at 50%. Notably, some tasks — including deconvolution, surface measurement, and voxel size reading — could not be solved by any model tested. A broader evaluation across 293 biomedical data science tasks found that standalone LLMs achieve under 40% accuracy, but an iterative agent approach — where the system executes code, observes errors, and refines its solution — raised accuracy to 74%10. These benchmark numbers will change as models improve, but they provide a realistic snapshot: AI-generated code is a useful starting point, not a finished product.
AI-assisted code generation has not reached the point where users without any programming understanding can reliably build complex analysis pipelines. Users still need foundational computational thinking — not necessarily memorized syntax, but the ability to decompose problems into discrete steps, recognize when an output looks wrong, and evaluate whether an approach is appropriate for their data. AI-assisted programming lowers the barrier to entry; it does not eliminate the need for scientific judgment about what the code should do.

title: 3  Large Language Models and AI Agents
section: 3.3 From Text Generation to Action: Function Calling and Tool Use
text:
3.3 From Text Generation to Action: Function Calling and Tool Use
A critical limitation of early LLMs was that they could only produce text. A researcher could ask ChatGPT how to segment nuclei in a DAPI image, and the model would generate a Python script — but the researcher still had to copy that code, set up the right software environment, install dependencies, debug errors, and run it themselves. The model was knowledgeable but unable to act. Function calling (also known as tool use) circumvented this barrier. Instead of merely describing what a user should do, an LLM can now invoke external tools, pass structured parameters, receive results, and reason about what to do next.

section: 3.3.2 From Fragmented Tools to a Universal Protocol
text:
3.3.2 From Fragmented Tools to a Universal Protocol
Function calling became an industry standard quickly — by early 2024, every major LLM provider supported structured tool invocation. Two subsequent developments made it considerably more powerful for scientific applications.
First, multimodal function calling (introduced with GPT-4o in May 2024) allowed a model to examine an image and call analysis tools in a single interaction. A researcher could upload a confocal image and ask “segment the nuclei,” and the model would both interpret the image visually and invoke the appropriate segmentation tool — combining perception with action.
Second, a key practical challenge was fragmentation: every tool provider defined its own interface format, making it difficult to connect a single agent to diverse software. Anthropic’s Model Context Protocol (MCP), announced in November 2024, addressed this by providing an open standard for connecting AI agents to external tools and data sources. MCP gives any AI model a universal way to discover and use any compatible tool — analogous to how USB standardized device connectivity. For microscopy, MCP means that a single agent could potentially access a microscope control system, an image analysis library, a literature database, and a model repository through the same protocol. By late 2025, MCP had been adopted as an industry-wide standard, with its donation to the Linux Foundation and support from major AI providers.
Together, these developments transformed function calling from a feature of individual chatbots into the backbone of AI agent systems. Current frontier models combine large context windows with sophisticated tool use, enabling agents to work with entire experimental datasets in a single session. The practical impact for microscopy is explored in Section 3.5.
